theory.title: Reports, Proposals and Executive Synthesis
theory.explanation: This mission develops advanced reports and proposals. Effective C2 communication requires writers and speakers to make purpose, audience, evidence and degree of certainty explicit. Analyse the context before choosing a register; distinguish established information from interpretation; organise complex material so that decisions and qualifications remain visible.
theory.tip: Use precise terminology, attribute claims, qualify uncertainty and make the requested action explicit.

patterns.label: Define purpose and audience
patterns.pattern: Identify what the audience needs to know or decide.
examples: State the decision required before presenting supporting detail.

patterns.label: Support and qualify
patterns.pattern: Connect each claim to evidence and state relevant limitations.
examples: The findings suggest a pattern, although the sample is not representative.

patterns.label: Structure for action
patterns.pattern: Use signposting, headings and explicit ownership.
examples: The recommendation is assigned to a named lead for review by an agreed date.

patterns.label: Review for integrity
patterns.pattern: Check terminology, attribution, tone and consistency.
examples: Distinguish verified outcomes from projected benefits.

content.passage:
A city transport office commissioned a proposal to improve late-evening bus reliability. The first draft opened with a detailed account of the consultation process, followed by several pages of technical options. Senior readers struggled to identify the decision being requested.

The revised document began with an executive summary that stated the problem, the preferred option, its estimated cost and the principal uncertainty. A short options table compared feasibility, expected benefit and implementation risk. The recommendation was linked to three measurable outcomes: fewer cancelled services, shorter average delays and improved passenger confidence.

The proposal also identified milestones and a contingency if driver recruitment fell behind schedule. It did not present the preferred option as risk-free; it explained why the benefits justified a staged pilot and specified when the office should review the evidence. The result was shorter, but more accountable: each recommendation had an owner, a rationale and a way to assess whether it had worked.
